(Surah 28: Al-Qasas)

(Meccan, though it is said that the exception is His saying: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ up to His saying: ﴿the ignorant﴾. It has eighty-eight verses.)

﴿Ta Sin Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ What pertains to these letters has already been discussed in summary, and in detail in similar places.

We recite to you (نَتْلُو عَلَيْكَ): that is, we read (it) through Jibril (peace be upon him). It is also possible that recitation (التِّلاوَة) is used metaphorically for revelation (التَّنْزِيل).

Of the news of Musa and Fir'awn (مِن نَبَإ مُوسى وفِرْعَوْنَ): the object of natlu (نَتْلُو). That is, we recite to you some of the news of the two of them.

With truth (بِالحَقِّ): this is connected to a omitted verb (مُتَعَلِّقٌ بِمَحْذُوفٍ). It may be a circumstantial clause (حال) from the subject of natlu, or from its object, or an adjective of its verbal noun (مَصْدَر), meaning: some of their news, (told) as those who are truthful, or as one who is characterized by truth, or a recitation characterized by truth.

For a people who believe (لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ): this is connected to natlu. Their being singled out for this, despite the generality of the call and the clarification for all, is because they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land⦆ This is a resumptive statement serving as an explanation of the summarized matter that was promised. Its opening with the emphatic particle (inna) is for the sake of affirming the content of what follows, meaning: he acted tyrannically and transgressed in the land of Egypt, and exceeded the known limits in wrongdoing and aggression.

﴿And made its people into sects⦆ That is, factions who support him in everything he wills of evil and corruption; or some of them support others in obeying him; or categories in his service, employing each category in a task and putting them to work in building, tilling, digging, and other arduous labors. Whoever he did not employ, he imposed the jizya (poll tax) upon. Or they were divided factions, among whom he stirred up enmity and hatred so that their word would not unite.

﴿Dividing a group of them⦆ These were the Children of Israel. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "made," or an attributive clause describing "sects," or a resumptive statement. His words, exalted be He, ﴿slaughtering their sons and sparing their women⦆ are a substitute (badal) for it. This occurred because a soothsayer told him: "A boy will be born among the Children of Israel who will end your kingdom at his hands." This was nothing but the extreme of his folly, for if the prophecy were true, what is the benefit of killing, and if it were false, what is its justification?

﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters⦆ That is, among those firmly established in corruption. Therefore he dared to commit such a grave act as killing the protected sons of the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace.

﴿And We wish to bestow favour﴾, that is, We would show grace, ﴿upon those who were deemed weak in the land﴾, in the manner mentioned, by saving them from His punishment. The present-tense form "nuridu" (we wish) is a narration of a past state (*hikayat hal madiyya*), and it is coordinated with "inna Fir'awn 'ala ... etc." (that Pharaoh exalted himself ... etc.), because both occur within the scope of the explanation of "al-naba'" (the report). Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to "yastad'if" (he weakens), with the subject supplied, meaning: Pharaoh weakens them, while We wish to bestow favour upon them. It is not necessary that the wish be concurrent with the weakening, nor that the thing wished for be concurrent with it, since the wish to bestow favour relates to the future. Yet God's favour upon them through deliverance, since it was about to occur (*fi sharaf al-wuqu'*), was permissible to treat as the concurrent actual event. Placing the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) in place of the pronoun (*al-damir*) serves to show the greatness of the blessing in the favour, by mentioning their previous state, which stands in contrast to it.

﴿And We shall make them imams﴾, to be followed in matters of religion, after they had been subordinate followers of others.

﴿And We shall make them the inheritors﴾ of everything that had been included within the dominion of Pharaoh and his people, an inheritance customary among them, as indicated by the definiteness of "al-warithin" (the inheritors). The mention of their inheritance is delayed after the mention of their being made imams, although the inheritance precedes it in time, because its rank is lower than imamate, and so that what follows is not separated from it, though it is among its accompaniments, namely His statement, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 6:

﴿And We shall establish them in the land﴾ ... etc. That is: We shall give them power over Egypt and Syria, so that they dispose of them as they wish. The original meaning of tamkin (establishment) is that you make for a thing a place in which it becomes firmly settled.

﴿And We shall show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts, from them﴾ That is: from among those who were oppressed.

﴿that which they were wary of﴾ and were striving to avert, namely the loss of their kingdom and their destruction at the hands of a boy born among them. It is also read as (yara) with a ya' and the following word in the nominative, as the subject (fa'iliyyah).

﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾ by inspiration or by a dream.

﴿to suckle him﴾ for as long as you are able to conceal him. ﴿And if you fear for him﴾ that the neighbours would perceive him when he cries and inform on him.

﴿then cast him into the yam﴾ into the sea, which is the Nile.

﴿And do not fear﴾ any loss for him by drowning, nor any harm. ﴿And do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you﴾ soon, in such a way that you will be safe with him.

﴿And We will make him one of the messengers.﴾ This clause is a justification for the prohibition against fear and grief. The choice of a nominal clause (jumla ismiyya), introduced by the particle of affirmation (harf al-tahqiq), is for the sake of emphasizing the certainty of its content, meaning: Indeed, We are certainly going to return him to you and make him one of the messengers without doubt.

It is related that one of the midwives appointed by Pharaoh over the pregnant women of the Children of Israel was a close friend of the mother of Moses (peace be upon him). She said to her: "Let your love for me benefit me today." So she attended to her, and when he fell onto the ground, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her, every joint of her body trembled, and his love entered her heart. Then she said: "I only came to you to receive your newborn and to inform Pharaoh, but I have found in my heart a love for your son such as I have not found for anyone else, so guard him." When she went out, Pharaoh's agents came, and she wrapped him in a cloth and threw him into a heated oven, not knowing what she was doing, because her mind had been confused. They searched but found nothing, and they departed, while she did not know where he was. Then she heard his crying from the oven and went to him. God, exalted is He, had made the fire cool and safe for him. When Pharaoh insisted on searching for the boys, God, exalted is He, revealed to her what He revealed.

It is also related that she nursed him for three months in an ark of papyrus (tabut min bardiyy), coated with pitch (qar) on the inside. And the particle "الفاءُ" (fa') in the saying of God, exalted is He:

(p-4) ﴿Fa-iltaqatahu āl Fir'awn﴾ is a fa' of consequence (faṣīḥa mufṣiḥa) that discloses its connection (ʿaṭf) to a clause that follows from what precedes it, namely the command to cast (the infant). The intervening clause has been omitted, relying on the indication of the situation and to signify the completeness of the speed of compliance. The sense is: "So she cast him into the river after she had placed him in the chest, just as she was commanded. Then the people of Pharaoh picked him up," that is, they took him, caring for him and preserving him from being lost. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: At that time Pharaoh had a daughter, and he had no child other than her, and she was among the dearest of people to him. She had a severe leprosy (baras) which the physicians were unable to cure. They said: "She will not be healed except from the direction of the sea, from which is taken something resembling a human, on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such an hour of such-and-such a month, when the sun rises. From its saliva one takes some and smears her leprosy with it, and she will be healed." When that day came, Pharaoh went out to a gathering he had on the bank of the Nile, and with him was his wife Asiya daughter of Muzahim ibn ʿUbayd ibn al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, who was the Pharaoh of Egypt in the time of Joseph the Righteous, peace be upon him. It was also said that she was from the Children of Israel, from the tribe of Moses, peace and blessings be upon him; and it was said that she was his paternal aunt, as related by al-Suhayli. Pharaoh's daughter came with her maidservants until she sat on the bank of the Nile. Suddenly there was a chest in the Nile, being struck by the waves, and it caught on a tree. Pharaoh said: "Bring it to me." They hastened with the boats and brought it before him. They tried to open it but could not, and they sought to break it but it overpowered them. Asiya looked and saw a light in the inside of the chest which no one but she saw. She worked on it and opened it, and behold, there was a small infant in his cradle, and behold, a light between his eyes, and he was sucking his thumb for milk. Then Allah the Exalted placed His love in the hearts of the people. Pharaoh's daughter bent to his saliva and smeared her leprosy with it, and she was healed at that very moment. It was also said that when she looked at his face she was healed. The deluded ones among Pharaoh's people said: "We think that this is the one we fear; he was cast into the sea out of fear of you, so kill him." Pharaoh resolved to kill him, but Asiya asked him to be granted to her, and he left him, as will come.

The lam in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Li-yakūna lahum ʿaduwwan wa-ḥazanan﴾ [so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief], is the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿāqiba), whose object is presented in the form of a purpose for their picking him up, likening its result to the aim that prompted it. It was also read as (ḥuznan), and both are dialects, like al-saqam and al-suqm. He, peace be upon him, was made the very essence of grief, to signify the strength of his causing their grief.

﴿Inna Fir'awna wa-Hamana wa-junudahuma kānū khāṭi'īn﴾ [Indeed Pharaoh, Haman and their hosts were sinners]. That is: in everything they do and everything they omit. So there is no wonder that they slaughtered the nobles by the thousands, and then took him to raise him so that he might grow and do to them what they were fearful of. It is related that in pursuit of him, peace be upon him, ninety thousand infants were slaughtered. Or they were wrongdoers, and Allah the Exalted punished them by making their enemy rise up at their hands. So the clause is parenthetical, to emphasize their error, or to explain the cause of what they were afflicted with. It was also read as (khāṭṭīn), taken as a lightened form of khāṭi'īn, or as meaning "those who transgress the right into wrong" (mutaʿaddīn al-ṣawāb ilā al-khaṭa').

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 9:

﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said﴾ i.e., to Pharaoh, when she took him out of the chest (tabut).

﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you﴾ i.e., he is a comfort of the eye for us, because when the two of them saw him, they loved him; or because of what was mentioned about his daughter's being cured of leprosy (baras) by his saliva. And in a hadith it is said that he (ﷺ) said: "For you, not for me." Had he said, "As he is for you," Allah the Exalted would have guided him as He guided her.

﴿Do not kill him﴾ She addressed him in the plural form out of reverence, so that he would support her in what she wants.

﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾ for in him are signs of good fortune (makhayil al-yumn) and indications of nobility (najabah), and that is because of the marks mentioned that she saw in him.

﴿Or we may adopt him as a son﴾ i.e., we may adopt him, for he is fit for that.

﴿While they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the family of Pharaoh. The sense is: the family of Pharaoh picked him up so that he would become for them an enemy and a source of grief, and his wife said such-and-such, while they did not perceive that they were in a great error in what they did, in taking him up, hoping for benefit from him, and adopting him. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh﴾ ... the verse, is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) placed between the two conjoined elements, to emphasize their error. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause relating to one of the two pronouns in "we adopt him," on the basis that the pronoun refers to the people, meaning: while they do not know that he belongs to others than us, and we have indeed adopted him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 10:

﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became empty﴾ (fārighan), devoid of reason (ṣifran min al-'aql), because of the fear and bewilderment that overwhelmed her when she heard of his falling into the hand of Pharaoh, in accordance with the words of God Most High: ﴿And their hearts were hollow (havā')﴾, i.e., void, with no reason in them. This is reinforced by the reading (fargh'an), from the expression "their blood is fargh between them," i.e., wasted (hadar). It has also been said: "empty" means free of worry and grief, due to the utmost trust in God Most High's promise, or because she heard that Pharaoh had shown affection toward him and adopted him. It was also read (Mu'sā) with a hamza, treating the damma on the letter preceding the waw (in the prepositional position) as if it were its own damma, so the hamza was added, as in the forms of ﴿If she had almost revealed him﴾ (in kādat latubdī bihi), i.e., she had almost disclosed Moses, meaning his affair and story, out of excessive bewilderment and astonishment, or out of joy at his adoption.

﴿Had We not fortified her heart﴾ with patience and steadfastness ﴿so that she might be among the believers﴾, i.e., those who affirm God Most High's promise, or among those who trust in His protection and not in Pharaoh's adoption and affection. This is the cause of the strengthening, and the answer to (law-lā, "had it not been for") is omitted, as the preceding context indicates it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 11:

﴿And she said to his sister﴾ — Maryam. The expression of her as his sister (peace be upon him), rather than saying "to his daughter," is to make clear the basis of the love which necessitates compliance with the command.

﴿Follow him﴾ — i.e., follow his trail and trace his news.

﴿Then she watched him﴾ — i.e., she saw him ﴿from afar﴾ — from a distance. It is also read ﴿ʿan junub﴾ with the nun sukun, and ﴿ʿan jānib﴾ (from a side), and all of them have the same meaning. ﴿And they did not perceive﴾ that she was following him and getting to know his condition, or that she was his sister.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 12:

﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾ That is: We prevented him from suckling from the nursing women. The word al-marad'i (المراضع) is the plural of murdi' (مُرْضِع), which refers to the woman who nurses; or it is murdi' (مُرْضِع), which denotes the act of nursing (al-rada'), or its place, meaning the breast.

﴿from before﴾ That is: before she (his sister) traced his trail (qassaha athara-hu).

﴿Then she said﴾ upon seeing that he would not accept the breast, and Pharaoh's concern for his matter, and their seeking someone whose breast he would accept.

﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will take care of him for you?﴾ That is: for your sake.

﴿and they will be sincere to him﴾ ﴿they will not fall short in nursing him and raising him.﴾ It is related that when Haman heard it from her, he said: "Indeed she knows him and his family, so seize her until she informs us of his condition." She said: "I only meant, and they are sincere to the king." So Pharaoh ordered her to bring someone who would nurse him, and she brought his mother. Musa was crying in Pharaoh's arms while he was soothing him, so he handed him to her. When he smelled her scent he became at ease, and he took her breast into his mouth. Pharaoh said: "Who are you to him, for he has refused every breast except yours?" She said: "I am a woman of pleasant scent and pleasant milk; no infant is brought to me but that he accepts me." (p-6) So he entrusted him to her hand and assigned a provision to her, and she returned with him to her house that same day. That is His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be comforted﴾ by the arrival of her son to her.

﴿And that she should not grieve﴾ over his separation, ﴿and that she might know that the promise of God﴾ — that is, all that He had promised her of his return and of making him one of the messengers — ﴿is true﴾, free of any falsehood, through witnessing part of it and inferring the rest from it.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that the matter is so, and so they doubt concerning it; or it may be that the primary purpose of the return was her knowledge of this, and everything else is secondary. And in it there is an allusion to what had escaped from her when she heard of his falling into the hand of Pharaoh.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 14:

﴿When he reached his full strength﴾, that is, the point beyond which his growth no longer increases. This is from thirty to forty years of age, for intellect then reaches maturity. It is related that no prophet was sent except at the age of forty.

﴿And he became firm﴾, that is, his stature became balanced, or his intellect did.

﴿We gave him judgment﴾, that is, prophethood (nubuwwa).

﴿And knowledge﴾ of the religion, or the knowledge of the wise and the scholars, and their dignified bearing (samt) before his prophethood, so that he would not say or do anything for which he would be deemed ignorant. This is more fitting to the arrangement of the narrative, because God made him a prophet after the migration (hijra) in the account of the return (al-muraja'a).

﴿And thus﴾, that is, in the same manner as what We did for Moses and his mother, ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾ for their goodness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 15:

﴿And he entered the city﴾ i.e., Egypt, from the palace of Pharaoh. It was said: Memphis (Manf), or Habin, or 'Ayn Shams, from its districts.

﴿at a time of unawareness of its people﴾ at a time when entering it was not customary, or when they did not expect him at that time. It was said: it was the time of midday rest (al-qaylulah), and it was said: between the two evening prayers (al-'isha'ayn).

﴿and he found in it two men fighting, one of his own party (shi'ah)﴾ i.e., one of those who supported him in his religion, and they were the Children of Israel.

﴿and the other of his enemy﴾ i.e., one of those who opposed him in religion, and they were the Copts (al-qibt). The phrase "this" (hadha) is in the sense of narration (al-hikayah).

﴿So the one who was of his party sought his help against the one who was of his enemy; so Moses struck him﴾ i.e., he asked him to come to his aid with support, as its construction with 'ala indicates. It was also read as (ista'anahu). ﴿so Moses struck him﴾ i.e., he struck the Copt with the joined fingers of his hand. It was also read as (fa-lakazahu), meaning he struck him on the chest with it.

﴿and he put an end to him﴾ i.e., he killed him. Its origin is ending his life, from the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We conveyed to him that decree﴾. ﴿He said: This is of the work of Satan﴾ because he had not been commanded to kill the disbelievers, or because he had been trusted among them, so it was not permissible for him to assassinate them. This does not detract from his infallibility (ismah), since it was a mistake. He only considered it to be of the work of Satan, called it wrongdoing (zulm), and sought forgiveness for it, following the practice of those brought near (al-muqarrabin) in magnifying whatever lapse came from them, even if it was among the least of minor sins.

﴿Indeed, he is an open enemy, misleading and manifest﴾ clearly manifest in enmity and in misguidance.

﴿He said﴾ Its placement between his two statements (ﷺ) shows the difference between them: this one is a private supplication and prayer, unlike the first.

﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself﴾ i.e., by killing him.

﴿So forgive me﴾ my sin.

﴿So He forgave him﴾ that, ﴿indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ i.e., the one who greatly exceeds in forgiving the sins of His servants and in showing mercy to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 17:

﴿He said: "My Lord, by that which You have bestowed upon me"﴾ either this is an oath with its answer omitted, meaning: "I swear by Your bestowal upon me of forgiveness that I will certainly repent."

﴿So never will I be﴾ after this, ever.

﴿a supporter (zahir) of the criminals﴾. The "ma" (in "bima") is for seeking compassion (istita'tf), meaning: "By the right of Your bestowal upon me, protect me, so that I will never be a helper to anyone whose assistance would lead to the sacred prohibitions (al-huram)." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he (peace be upon him) did not make an exception, so he was tested with it a second time. This supports the first interpretation. It has also been said: its meaning is, "By what You have bestowed upon me of strength, I will help Your friends, so I will never use it in aiding Your enemies."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 18:

﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful,﴾ watching out for retaliation (qisas), or for the agents (al-ajnad).

﴿So behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was calling out to him for help.﴾ That is: he was calling on him for aid, raising his voice (min al-sarakh), i.e., crying out.

﴿Musa said to him, "Indeed, you are clearly a misguided one (ghawiyy mubin)."﴾ That is: evidently misguided (bayyin al-ghawayah). You have caused the killing of a man, and now you are fighting another.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 28, verse 19:**

﴿So when he intended﴾ Musa ﴿to strike the one who was an enemy to both of them﴾, that is, to both Musa and the Israelite, since the man was not of their religion, and because the Copts were enemies of the Children of Israel in general. It is also read as (yabtushu) with a *ḍamma* on the *ṭā'*, i.e., *yabṭush* (a variant recitation, *qirā'ah*).

﴿He said﴾, that is, the Israelite, thinking that he (ﷺ) was about to strike him, as his calling him *ghūban* (an insult meaning one who has gone astray, *ghawī*) suggests.

﴿O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?﴾ They said: When the Copt heard the Israelite's words, he knew that Musa was the one who had killed that Pharaonic man. So he went to Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and informed him of this, and Fir'awn ordered that Musa, peace be upon him, be killed. It is said that the Copt himself said it.

﴿You only wish﴾, that is, *mā turīd* (you wish nothing other than).

﴿to be a jabbār (tyrant) in the land﴾, who does whatever he wishes of striking and killing and does not consider the consequences. It is also said: one who is arrogant and does not humble himself before the command of God, exalted is He.

﴿And you do not wish to be among the reformers﴾ between people, by word and by deed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 20:

﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city﴾ i.e., one who was from its far end, or he came from its far end.

﴿Running﴾ i.e., hastening. It is an attribute of "a man." Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from him, on the basis that the prepositional phrase is an attribute of him, not dependent on "came," since its specification attaches it to the definite (ma'arif). It was said: he is the believer of the family of Pharaoh (Mu'min Al Fir'awn), whose name was Hizqil; it was said: Sham'un; and it was said: Sham'an.

﴿He said: "O Musa, indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you"﴾ i.e., they are consulting with one another on account of you, for each of those consulting is bidding the others (ya'tamiru), and conspiring (ya'tamiru).

﴿So leave﴾ i.e., from the city.

﴿Indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisors﴾ The lam is for explanation (lil-bayan) (p-8), because the object of the relative clause (ma'mul al-silah) does not precede it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 21:

﴿So he went out from it﴾, i.e., from the city.

﴿Fearful, watching out﴾ for the pursuit of those seeking him. ﴿He said: "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people"﴾, i.e., rescue me from them, and protect me from their pursuit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 22:

﴿When he turned his face toward Madyan﴾ That is, toward Madyan. It was the town of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. It was named after Madyan ibn Ibrahim. It was not under the authority of Pharaoh, and the distance between it and Egypt was eight days' journey.

﴿He said: "It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right way."﴾ This was out of reliance upon God Most High and confidence in His good provision, for he did not know the roads. Three paths presented themselves to him, and he took the middle one, while the seekers who came after him set out on the other two. It is also said that he went out barefoot, living only on the leaves of trees, and by the time he arrived the soles of his feet had worn away. It is also said that an angel came to him on a horse, carrying a staff (ʿanazah), and set off with him toward Madyan.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 23:

﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ — that is, he reached it. It is a well from which they used to give water. ﴿He found upon it﴾ — that is, above its edge — ﴿a community﴾, a dense group ﴿of people watering﴾ — that is, their livestock.

﴿And he found, besides them﴾ — that is, in a place lower down than them —

﴿two women holding back﴾ — that is, keeping back what they had of sheep from advancing to the well, lest they mix with their flocks, since there was no benefit in advancing.

﴿He said﴾ — peace be upon him — to them, when he saw them in the state they were in of holding back and keeping apart: ﴿"What is your business?"﴾ — what is your affair in what you are doing of holding back and keeping apart? Why do you not take up the watering as these people do? ﴿They said: "We cannot water until the shepherds send off [their flocks]."﴾ That is: our custom is not to water until the shepherds have driven their flocks away from the water after they have quenched their thirst; this is out of inability to compete with them and caution against mixing with men, not that we do not water today up to that point. The omission of the object of watering, holding back and sending off is because the purpose is to explain these actions themselves, for it is they that prompted Moses, peace be upon him, to the kindness he did for them. He had mercy on them only because they were holding back out of weakness and chastity, and the others were heedless of them while watering; he did not have mercy on them merely for their driving sheep and their watering camels, for example. It has been read: (we do not water) from the causative form, and (yuṣdira) from the intransitive form, and (al-ru'ā') with a damma on the rā': it is a collective noun like al-rukhā', whereas al-ri'ā' is a regular plural like ṣiyām and qiyām. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And our father is a very old man"﴾ is a clearing of themselves to him, peace be upon him, regarding their taking up the watering themselves, as if they said: "We are two weak women, kept modest, unable to compete with men and crowd against them, and we have no man to take charge of this; our father is a very old man whom old age has weakened, so we must delay the watering until people have had their needs from the water."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 24:**

﴿So he watered [the flocks] for them﴾, out of compassion for them. The discussion concerns the omission of its object, as was mentioned just above. It is narrated that the shepherds used to place on the mouth of the well a stone that only seven men could lift. It is also said: ten; it is also said: forty; and it is also said: a hundred. He lifted it alone, despite the exhaustion, the injury and the hunger he was suffering from. Perhaps (p-9) upon him be peace pushed in among them to water [the flocks] for the two women, so they put the stone back over the well to prevent him, upon him be peace, from doing so. For the apparent meaning is that upon him be peace, after witnessing their condition, hastened to water [the flocks] for them. It has also been narrated that he pushed them away from the water until he had watered [the flocks] for the two women. It is also said that there was another well nearby, over which was the aforementioned rock. It is narrated that upon him be peace asked them for a bucket of water, and they gave him their bucket, saying: "Draw with it." It could be drawn only by forty men, but he drew with it, poured it into the trough, and invoked blessing. Then he watered their flocks and sent them back.

﴿Then he withdrew to the shade﴾ that was there.

﴿And said: "My Lord, truly I am in need of whatever good You send down to me"﴾. That is: whatever thing You send down to me, ﴿of good﴾, whether great or small. Most commentators took it to mean food, by the indication of the context.

﴿Poor﴾, that is: in need. Because it contains the meaning of a request and a plea, the lam of support (lam al-di'ama, the lam that reinforces the verb) was brought to strengthen the action. It is also said that the meaning is: "[I am in need of] whatever great good You send down to me, which is the good of both abodes," for I have become poor in this world, because he had been in ease of living with Pharaoh. He, upon him be peace, said this to express gratitude and thankfulness for that.

﴿فَجاءَتْهُ إحْداهُما﴾ It is said: she was the elder of the two, and her name was Ṣafūrā' or Ṣafrā'. It is also said: she was the younger, and her name was Ṣufayrā'. That is, she came to him immediately after they had returned to their father. It is narrated that when the two of them returned to their father before the other shepherds, and their sheep were full-uddered and fat, he said to them: "What has made you hasten?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had mercy on us and watered (our flock) for us." So he said to one of them: "Go and call him to me." The words of Allah, ﴿تَمْشِي﴾ ("walking"), are a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to the subject of ﴿جاءَتْ﴾ ("came"). The words of Allah, ﴿عَلى اسْتِحْياءٍ﴾ ("with modesty"), are connected to an implied element, and it is a ḥāl relating to the pronoun in ﴿تَمْشِي﴾. That is: she came to him walking, being with modesty. Its meaning is that she was modest in both states, the walking and the coming together, not only at the moment of coming. The indefinite form of ﴿اسْتِحْياءٍ﴾ is for emphasis (tafkhīm, magnifying). It is said: she came to him ﴿مُتَخَفِّرَةً﴾ (mutakhaffiraẓatan), meaning very shy. It is also said: she covered herself with the sleeve of her garment.

﴿قالَتْ﴾ ("she said") is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf), built upon a question that arises from the narration of her coming to him, peace be upon him. It is as if it were said: "What did she say to him, peace be upon him?" So it is said: she said, ﴿إنَّ أبِي يَدْعُوكَ لِيَجْزِيَكَ أجْرَ ما سَقَيْتَ لَنا﴾ ("Indeed my father invites you, that he may reward you the wage for having watered (the flock) for us"). That is, as a recompense for your watering for us. She attributed the invitation to her father and gave the reason as recompense, so that her speech would not give rise to suspicion. In this is evidence of perfect intellect, modesty, and chastity, which is not hidden. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, responded to her, and they set off, while she was ahead of him. The wind pressed her garment against her body, so she described (her body to him). He said to her: "Walk behind me and direct me to the path." She did so until they reached the house of Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both.

﴿فَلَمّا جاءَهُ وقَصَّ عَلَيْهِ القَصَصَ﴾ That is: what had happened to him of the narrated account. The word ﴿القَصَصَ﴾ is a maṣdar (verbal noun) which has been used to name the object, like ʿIlal (illnesses/causes used for the diseases).

﴿قالَ لا تَخَفْ نَجَوْتَ مِنَ القَوْمِ الظّالِمِينَ﴾ What appears from the apparent sense of this noble text is that Musa, peace be upon him, responded to the one who invited him without hesitation, in order to seek blessing by seeing Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and to be strengthened by his opinion, not in order to take a wage for his kindness, as she herself stated. Do you not see what is narrated: when Shu'ayb set food before him, he said: "We are a household that does not sell our religion for the dust of the earth in gold, nor do we take a price for kindness," and he did not partake of it, until Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said: "This is our custom with everyone who stays with us." Then he partook of it afterwards, by way of accepting a kindness that was initiated (by the host). How could it not be so, when he had related his story to him and informed him that he was from the house of prophethood, from the descendants of Ya'qub, peace be upon him? Someone like him is worthy of being hosted and honored, especially in the house of a prophet among the prophets of Allah, the Exalted, peace be upon them. It is said: it is not objectionable on his part, peace be upon him, to accept the wage because of the compulsion of poverty and destitution. It is narrated from ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib that he, peace be upon him, raised his voice in his supplication so that she would hear it, and for this reason it was said to him: ﴿"That he may reward you..."﴾ etc. Perhaps he, peace be upon him, only did this so that it would be a means to his summoning (her father), not to securing the wage.

"Said one of them": she is the one who summoned him to their father, and she is the one whom Moses (peace be upon them both) later married.

"O father, hire him": that is, to tend the sheep and take charge of their affairs.

"Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy one": this is a reason that serves as a proof that he deserves to be hired. For emphasis, "the best" (khayra) is made the subject of "indeed" (inna), and the verb is put in the past form to indicate that he is a trustworthy person who has been tested. It is related that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) said to her: "How do you know of his strength and trustworthiness?" So she mentioned what she had witnessed from him (peace be upon him): his lifting of the stone, his drawing of the bucket, and that he lowered his head until she conveyed his message to him, and she instructed her to walk behind him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 27:

﴿He said: "I intend to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you hire yourself out to me"﴾ That is: that you be a hired worker (ajir) for me; or that you reward me (tuthibani) from "ajjartu kadha" (I paid such-and-such), when "athbtahu iyyahu" (I gave him its reward) is used. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿eight years﴾ — according to the first meaning, it is an adverb of time (zarf); and according to the second, it is a direct object (maf'ul bihi) with an elided modifier (mudaf), that is: "the tending of eight years" (ri'yata thamani hijaj). It is reported from al-Mubarrad that it is said: "ajjartu dari wa mamlukí" (without the alif, in the sense of "I rented out my house and my slave") and "ajartu" (with the alif, mamdud), and the first is more common. According to this, the second object is elided, and the meaning is: "on condition that you hire yourself out to me," and His saying, exalted is He, "eight years," is an adverb of time, as in the first case.

﴿But if you complete ten﴾ in service and work.

﴿then it is from you﴾ That is: then it is from you, by way of bounty (tafaddul), not from me, by way of obligation upon you. This is from Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, a presentation of his opinion to Musa, and a solicitation from him for the contract, not a concluding of it, and an affirmation of it in action.

﴿And I do not intend to burden you﴾ by imposing the completion of the ten, or by scrupulous scrutiny regarding the observance of times and the exacting of works. The derivation of "mashaqqah" (hardship) is from "shiqq" (split), for what is difficult for you splits upon you through your belief in its being beyond your capacity, and your opinion is divided in undertaking it.

﴿You will find me, God willing, among the righteous﴾ in good dealing, gentleness of manner, and fulfilment of covenant. His intention, upon him be blessings and peace, by the exception (istithna') was seeking blessing through it (al-tabarruk bihi), and committing his affair to God's granting of success, not making his righteousness conditional upon God's will.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 28:

﴿He said: "That is between me and you."﴾ It is a subject and predicate construction, meaning: that which you have said and covenanted with me concerning it, and stipulated with me upon it, stands and is established between all of us; none of us departs from it. Neither am I free of what was stipulated upon me, nor are you free of what you stipulated upon yourself. And the words of the Exalted: ﴿whichever of the two terms﴾ mean: the more or the less of them.

﴿I fulfil﴾ means: I will have completed it for you by performing the service in it.

﴿So there shall be no injustice against me﴾ is an explicit statement of the intended meaning and an affirmation of the matter of choice. That is: there shall be no injustice against me by seeking more than what I have fulfilled of the two terms. The generalisation of the negation of injustice to both terms, in the context of the stipulation, is made while injustice does not arise at all in the more of them, for the purpose of equating them in the negation. (p-11) That is: just as I shall not be asked for more than ten, I shall not be asked for more than eight. Or: whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there is no sin upon me, meaning that just as there is no sin upon me in fulfilling the more, there is no sin upon me in fulfilling only the less.

It has also been read as ﴿أيَّ الأجَلَيْنِ ما قَضَيْتُ﴾ (whichever of the two terms I fulfil), where "ما" is superfluous, for the emphasis of the fulfilment, just as it is superfluous in the first reading for the emphasis of indefiniteness, that is, its generality. It has also been read as "أيْما" with the "ya" vowelless, like the saying of one who said:

"I waited for Nasr and the two Simaks, whichever of them has poured its rains upon me."

﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾ of the conditions that exist between us. ﴿Wakil (Guardian)﴾ means witness and guardian, so there is no way for either of us to depart from it at all. What is related of the two of them, peace be upon them, is not the complete account of what passed between them in speech concerning the concluding of the marriage contract, the contract of hire, and their executing them; rather it is an indication of what was agreed upon in its execution, as the course of the story requires in summary, without addressing in detail the obligations of the two contracts in that law.

It is related that when they had concluded the contract, Shu'ayb said to Musa, peace be upon them both: "Enter that house and take a staff from those staffs." (The staffs of the prophets, peace be upon them, were with him.) So he took a staff which Adam, peace be upon him, had brought down from Paradise, and the prophets had continued to inherit it until it came into the possession of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. He touched it, and he was blind, so he was miserly with it and said: "Take another." But nothing came into his hand except it, seven times, so he knew that it had a status. It was also said: Jibril, peace be upon him, took it after the death of Adam, peace be upon him, and it remained with him until he met Musa with it at night. It was also said: an angel in the form of a man deposited it with Shu'ayb, and he commanded his daughter to bring him a staff; she brought it to him, and he returned it seven times, and nothing came into her hand except it, so he gave it to him. Then he regretted it, because it was a deposit, and he followed him, and they disputed over it, and they agreed that the first one to appear should judge between them. The angel came to them and said: "Throw it down; whoever lifts it, it is his." The old man tried to lift it but could not, and Musa, peace be upon him, lifted it.

It is related from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was only a staff of wood which he picked up at random. It is related from al-Kalbi, may Allah have mercy on him, that the tree from which he was called was the tree of al-'awsaj (a thorny shrub), and from it was his staff. When morning came, Shu'ayb, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them both, said to him: "When you reach the fork of the road, do not take the right-hand path, for although the pasture there is more abundant, there is a serpent there which I fear for you and for the sheep." The sheep took the right-hand path, and he could not restrain them, so he walked following their tracks, and there was lush grass and fertile land the like of which had never been seen, and he slept. Then the serpent came, and the staff fought it until it killed it, and it returned to Musa's side, bloodied. When he saw it bloodied and the serpent slain, he was pleased by that. When he returned to Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, he touched the sheep and found their bellies full and their milk abundant. Musa, peace be upon him, informed him of the matter, and he rejoiced and knew that Musa and the staff had a status. He said to him: "I have given you from the offspring of this year's flock every speckled and spotted one," and he called him, and it was revealed to him in a dream: "Strike the watering place of the sheep with your staff," and he did so; then he watered them, and not one of them missed but it gave birth to speckled and spotted young. Thus he fulfilled to him his condition.

And the "fa'" in the words of the Exalted:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 29:**

﴿When Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ *fa* here is a *fasiha* (a particle indicating an implied omitted clause). That is, they concluded the two contracts, and Moses carried out what he had committed himself to, so when he had completed the term.

﴿And he set out with his family﴾ toward Egypt, with the permission of Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, fulfilled the more complete of the two terms, and stayed with him for ten years after that. Then he resolved to return to Egypt, so he asked his permission for that (p-12), and he granted it, and he set out with his family.

﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the Mount﴾ meaning he saw it from the direction facing the Mount (*al-Tur*).

﴿a fire. He said to his family, "Wait here, indeed I have perceived a fire; perhaps I may bring you news from it"﴾ meaning news of the road, for they had lost their way. ﴿Or a brand﴾ meaning a thick piece of wood, whether or not there was fire at its tip. As one of them said:

*Lovers of Layla's firewood went out at night seeking for her thick sticks, neither mixed nor rotten.*

And he said:

*He cast onto a flame of fire a brand, its heat and blaze intense upon it.*

For this reason, the verse specifies with His words ﴿from the fire﴾. It has been read with a kasra on the *jim* (جَذْوَة, *jadhwa*) and with a damma on it, and both are dialectal forms.

﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾ meaning that you may warm yourselves by its heat.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 30:

﴿When he came to it﴾, i.e., the fire that he had perceived (ānasahā).

﴿He was called from the right side of the valley﴾, i.e., the call came to him from the right-hand side relative to Musa, peace be upon him.

﴿In the blessed spot﴾ is connected to "the side" (shāṭi'), or is a complement (ṣilah) for "was called."

﴿From the tree﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the side" (shāṭi'), because it was growing on the side.

﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾. This, although it differs in wording from what is in Ta-Ha and an-Naml, nevertheless agrees with it in the intended meaning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 31:

﴿And that you throw down your staff﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with the "an" of "Ya Musa" (that: "O Musa"), and both are explanatory (mufassir) of "nuwdiya" (he was called). The "fa" (fa') in the words of the Exalted, ﴿So when he saw it moving﴾, is the fa' of eloquent expression (fasiha mufsiha), revealing clauses that have been omitted, relying on the situation (al-hal) to indicate them, and to signal the extreme speed with which what they signify is realised. The meaning is: so he threw it, and it became a serpent, and it moved, so when he saw it moving, ﴿as though it were a jann﴾, that is, in the speed of its movement together with the extreme enormity of its body.

﴿And he turned back fleeing﴾, that is, routed out of fear.

﴿And he did not look back﴾, that is, he did not return.

﴿O Musa﴾, that is, it was said: O Musa, ﴿come forward and do not fear. Indeed, you are of those secure﴾ from dangers, for indeed, ﴿those sent do not fear in My presence﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 32:

﴿Insert your hand into your pocket﴾, i.e., put it into it.

﴿It will come out white, without blemish﴾, i.e., without defect.

﴿And draw your arm close to your side﴾, i.e., your two outstretched hands, so that you may protect yourself by them from the serpent, like one who is frightened and alarmed, by placing the right hand under the left armpit and the left under the right, or by placing both of them into the pocket. This would be a repetition for another purpose: that it should be done in the face of the enemy as a display of boldness, and a beginning of the manifestation of a miracle. It is also permissible that "drawing close" (al-damm) is meant as steadfastness and firmness at the moment the staff turns into a serpent, a metaphor taken from the state of the bird: when it is afraid, it spreads its wings, and when it is secure and at rest, it folds them back to itself. ﴿Because of the terror﴾, i.e., on account of fear. That is: when fear overtakes you, do this as an exercise in fortitude and self-control. It is also read with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the ha', and also with a damma on both; all are dialectal forms (lughat).

﴿These two﴾ refers to the staff and the hand. It is also read with a shadda on the nun: the unshadda form is the dual of dhaka, and the shadda form is the dual of dhalika.

﴿Are two proofs﴾, i.e., two clear arguments. Burhan is on the pattern fu'lan, from their saying abrahar-rajulu, "the man brought proof," from their saying barahar-rajulu, "the man became white." It is said of a white woman: barha' and barharaha. Its counterpart is the naming of an argument sultan, from al-salit, which is oil, because of its illumination. It is also said that it is fu'lal, from their saying barhana (to prove). The "min" in His saying, ﴿from your Lord﴾, is related to an omitted element which is an attribute of burhanan, meaning: they are originating ﴿from Him, the Exalted﴾; ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, arriving and terminating at them.

﴿Indeed they are a people who have been defiant﴾, i.e., who have gone beyond the limits of wrongdoing and transgression, so they were deserving that We send you to them with these two dazzling miracles.

Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on surah 28, verse 33:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I killed a man among them, and I fear that they will kill me"﴾ in retaliation for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 34:

﴿And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent in tongue than me, so send him with me as a helper (ridan)﴾ i.e., as an aide. It is originally the name of that which is helped with, like "difu'" (warmth), and it was recited as "radan" with the light pronunciation (al-takhfif).

﴿He will confirm me﴾ by clarifying the truth, establishing the proof by explaining it, and exposing the doubt as false.

﴿Indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾ and my tongue does not comply with me at the time of disputation. It was also said: the meaning is the people's confirmation of him, through establishing and clarifying his (Harun's) argument, but it is attributed to him in the manner of attributing an act to its cause. It was also recited as "yasduqni" with the jussive (jazm), on the basis that it is the answer to the imperative.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 35:

﴿He said: "We will strengthen your arm through your brother."﴾ That is: We will strengthen you through him, for a person's strength lies in the might of the hand for handling affairs; for this reason he is referred to by the hand, and its might by the might of the arm.

﴿And We will give you both authority﴾ That is: domination and dominance. It was said: proof (ḥujjah), but that is not the case.

﴿So they shall not reach you﴾ by seizing power or by argument.

﴿by Our signs﴾ This is connected to an omitted verb which is stated explicitly in other places, meaning: "Go by Our signs." Or it is connected to "We will give" (najʿalu), meaning: "We will empower you by Our signs." Or it is connected to the sense of "they shall not reach" (lā yaṣilūna), meaning: "you will prevail over them by means of them." It was said: it is an oath, and its answer is "they shall not reach." It was also said: it is an explanation of "the victors" (al-ghālibūn) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿You two and those who follow you are the victors﴾, in the sense that it is a relative clause (ṣilah) for what it explains, or a relative clause for it on the basis that the "lām" (in al-ghālibūn) is for definiteness, not in the sense of "alladhī" (who).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 36:

﴿So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs﴾ i.e., clear in their indication of the truth of Moses' message from Him, exalted is He. What is meant by them are the staff and the hand, for these are the two that Moses, peace be upon him, displayed at that time. The expression of them in the plural form has had its secret explained in Surah Ta-Ha.

﴿They said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic"﴾ i.e., fabricated magic, which had not been performed before this, the like of it; or magic that you yourself perform and then attribute falsely to Allah, exalted is He; or magic described as fabrication, like all other kinds of magic.

﴿And we have not heard of this﴾ i.e., of the magic, or of the claim to prophethood.

﴿among our forefathers of old﴾ i.e., occurring in their days.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 37:

﴿And Moses said: "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him."﴾ He means by this himself. It is also read as "qāla" without a waw (wa), because it is a reply to their statement. The reason for the conjunction (al-'atf) is that the intent is to relate both statements, so that the listener may weigh them against each other and distinguish the sound of them from the corrupt.

﴿And whoever will have the good outcome of the abode﴾ That is: the praiseworthy outcome in the abode. The abode is this world (al-dunya), and its original outcome is the Garden (al-Jannah), because it was created as a passage (majaz) to the Hereafter and as a field (mazra'ah) for it. What is intended in its own right (bi'l-dhat) from it is the reward (al-thawab); as for punishment ('iqab), it is among the consequences of the deeds of the disobedient and the evil doings of the misguided. It is also read as "yakūnu" with a yā' (the second-person form with the initial letter yā' of the third person). 

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers do not prosper.﴾ That is: they do not succeed in attaining what they seek, nor do they escape what they fear.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 38:

﴿And Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself."﴾ He, the accursed one, said this after he had gathered the magicians and taken up the challenge of opposition, and so there occurred what occurred concerning them.

﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay﴾, i.e., make bricks (ajurr, sing. ajurr, fired brick).

﴿And build for me﴾ from them ﴿a tower (sarh)﴾, i.e., a lofty palace.

﴿That I may look upon the god of Moses﴾. It is as though he imagined that if (God) existed, He would be a body in the sky, to which ascent could be made. Then he said: ﴿And indeed, I think him to be among the liars﴾. Or he intended to build for himself an observatory (rasad) from which he could watch the positions of the stars, so that he might see whether among them was anything indicating the sending of a messenger and the change of his dynasty. It is also said: the intended meaning of the negation of knowledge is the negation of the known object, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Will you inform God of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?﴾, for its meaning is "of what is not in them." This pertains to the special characteristics of active knowledge (al-'ulum al-fi'liyyah), for it necessarily entails the realization of its objects, so that the non-existence of the objects follows from the non-existence of the knowledge; this does not apply to receptive knowledge (al-'ulum al-infi'aliyyah). It is said: the first to make fired brick was Pharaoh. Therefore he commanded that it be made in a manner that includes teaching the craft, together with what is in it of exaltation (of himself); and for this reason he called Haman by name with "ya" in the middle of the speech.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 39:

﴿And he became arrogant, he and his soldiers, in the land﴾ the land of Egypt.

﴿without right﴾ without any entitlement.

﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ by resurrection for recompense. It is also read with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the jim, from raja'a, ruju'an (to return); the first reading is from raja'a, raj'an, and it is the more fitting to the context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 40:

﴿So We seized him and his hosts﴾, right after they had reached the utmost limits of disbelief and insolence.

﴿So We cast them into the sea﴾. Its detailed account has already passed. In it there is, clearly, an exaltation of the magnitude of the seizing and its awfulness, and a belittling of those seized and cast away, which is not hidden. It is as if He, exalted is He, seized them together with their multitude in one palm and threw them into the sea. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾, and ﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾, and He made it clear to people so that they might take warning from it.

﴿And We made them﴾, that is, We appointed them in their time.

﴿Leaders who call﴾ people ﴿to the Fire﴾, meaning to that which leads to it, namely disbelief and sins. That is, they are exemplars whom the people of misguidance follow, since they directed their choice toward attaining that state. It was also said: (p-15) We named them leaders, callers to the Fire, as in His saying: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾. On this view, the most fitting reading is that the "making" happens after them, among the nations, and that the calling is to the Fire itself. It was also said: the meaning of "making" is the withholding of divine graces (lutf, the divine assistance that turns a person away from misguidance).

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ by repelling the punishment from them in any way whatsoever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 42:

﴿And We made them follow up in this world with a curse﴾: expulsion and removal from mercy. And "a curse" (la'nan) from those who curse, since the angels, upon them be peace, and the believers, generation after generation, never cease to curse them.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾: among those expelled and removed far away. It is also said: among those marked with a hideous sign, such as blueness of the eyes and blackness of the face. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It is said: "Qabbahahu Allah" and "qabahahu," when one makes him ugly. Abu 'Ubayda said: "among the despised" means "among the destroyed." As for "on the Day of Resurrection," it is either connected to "the despised," with the lam being the definite article and not in the sense of "alladhi" (who), or it is connected to an omitted verb that this explains, as if it were said: "They will be despised on the Day of Resurrection, like what your deeds deserved, [being] among those who are wicked."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 43:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ That is: the Torah.

﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ They are the peoples of Noah, Hud, Salih and Lot, peace be upon them. The specification that the giving of it came after their destruction is to indicate the pressing need that called for it, as a preparation for what follows concerning the need that called for the sending down of the Noble Qur'an upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). For the destruction of the former generations was among the causes of the effacement of the landmarks of the sharia (shara'i', divine laws) and the obliteration of its traces and rulings, which lead to the disruption of the order of the world and the corruption of the conditions of nations, and these call for a new legislation, by establishing the principles that remain throughout the ages, arranging the branches that change with the changing eras, and reminding of the conditions of the past nations, which is a cause for taking heed. It is as if it were said: And We certainly gave Moses the Torah at a time when there was a need for its giving.

﴿as insights for mankind﴾ That is: lights for their hearts, by which they perceive the realities and distinguish between truth and falsehood, since they had been utterly blind to understanding and perception. For insight (basirah) is the light of the heart by which one gains insight, just as sight (basar) is the light of the eye by which one sees.

﴿and guidance﴾ That is: guidance to the laws and rulings which are the paths of Allah the Exalted.

﴿and mercy﴾ in that whoever acts upon it attains the mercy of Allah the Exalted. The accusative of all of these is in the circumstantial (hal) position relative to "the Book," on the basis that they are themselves the insights, the guidance and the mercy, or by omitting a modifier, i.e., possessing insights... etc. It has also been said that they are in the position of purpose (ʿilla), i.e., We gave him the Book for the sake of insights, guidance and mercy.

﴿so that they may remember﴾ so that they would be in a state from which remembrance is hoped for. The verification of the discussion on this has passed at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying, the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 44:

﴿And you were not on the western side﴾ This begins an explanation that the revelation of the Noble Qur'an likewise took place at a time when there was the greatest need for it, and when wisdom absolutely required it. It has been stated, in confirming that it is a true revelation from God, Mighty and Majestic, by showing that standing upon the details of the circumstances described is not possible (p-16) except through witnessing them, or learning from one who witnessed them. Since both of these were absent, it becomes clear that it is, without doubt, by revelation from the Knower of the unseen, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would take charge of Mary...﴾ ... the verse. That is: "And you were not on the side of the western mountain, or the western place where the appointed time occurred," with the noun elided and the adjective placed in its position; or "the western side," with the noun attached to the adjective, like "the Friday mosque" (masjid al-jami').

﴿When We decreed to Moses the command﴾ That is: We charged him, and We confirmed the matter of his prophethood through revelation and the giving of the Torah.

﴿Nor were you among the witnesses﴾ That is: among those who witnessed the revelation, namely the seventy chosen for the appointed time, so that you might have seen what happened to Moses at his appointed time, and the scribes of the Torah writing for him on the tablets, and then informed the people of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 45:

﴿But We produced generations⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ —﴾ That is: but We created many generations between your time and the time of Musa.

﴿so the age grew long for them⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ —﴾ and the period stretched out, so the sharia (sacred law) and the rulings changed, and the reports became obscure to them, especially to the latest of them. The situation required a new legislation, so We revealed to you. The omitted element has been left out, being sufficiently indicated by what necessitates it and points to it. His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And you were not a dweller among the people of Madyan⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ —﴾ negate the possibility that his (ﷺ) knowledge of the story came by hearing it from one who witnessed it; that is: you were not residing among the people of Madyan, [among those who followed] Shu'ayb and the believers in him. His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿reciting to them⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ —﴾ that is: you recite to the people of Madyan, by way of learning from them.

﴿Our verses⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ —﴾ which speak of the story, are either a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in thawiyan, or a second predicate for kunta.

﴿But We were senders⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ —﴾ of you, and revealers to you of those verses and their like.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 46:

﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount (al-Tur) when We called [Moses]﴾, that is: at the time of Our calling Moses, ﴿"Indeed I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds"﴾, and of Our appointing him as a prophet (istinba') and Our sending him to Pharaoh.

﴿But it is a mercy from your Lord﴾, that is: but We sent you with the Qur'an, which states what has been mentioned and other things, as a great mercy from Us to you and to mankind. It has been said: "We taught you," and it has been said: "We informed you of that," but this is not the correct meaning, as you will come to know. The shift (iltifat) to the name "the Lord" serves to indicate the reason for the mercy and to honor him, peace and blessings be upon him, by the addition (of the name "your Lord"). The omitted element (al-mustadrak) has been left unmentioned here, with mention of what necessitates it from the side of the Exalted One, just as in the first part he left it unmentioned with mention of what necessitates it from the side of the people. He made it explicit between the two, as a specification of what is intended and as an indication that it is also what is meant in both. How excellent is the wording of the revelation (lillah dar sha'n al-tanzil). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that you may warn a people﴾ is connected to the verb that is explained by the mercy, so it is what we mentioned of his sending, peace and blessings be upon him, with the Qur'an, definitively, because the warning is the thing being explained, not the teaching of what has been mentioned. It was also read as "rahmatun" (رَحْمَةٌ) in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to whom no warner had come before you﴾ is a qualifying clause (sifah) for "qawman" (a people), meaning: no warner had come to them because they were in an interval (fatrah) between you and Jesus, which lasted five hundred and fifty years, or between you and Isma'il, based on the view that the call of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, was specific to the Children of Israel.

﴿So that they may be mindful﴾, that is: that they may take admonition from your warning. The change of the sequence of events between (p-17) the decree of the command and the sojourn among the people of Madyan. The vocative (nida') serves as an alert that each of these is an independent proof that his narration, peace and blessings be upon him, of the story is through divine revelation. Had the negation of his sojourn among the people of Madyan been mentioned first, then the negation of his presence at the calling, then the negation of his presence at the decree of the command, as would accord with the actual sequence of events, it might have been supposed that all of them are one single proof of what has been mentioned, as has passed in surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 47:

﴿And had it not been that a calamity should befall them﴾ i.e., a punishment.

﴿for what their hands have sent forth﴾ i.e., what they have committed of disbelief and sins.

﴿then they would say﴾ is a conjunction with "tusibahum" (should befall them), falling within the scope of "lawla" (had it not been) of prevention, on the principle that what follows it is negated by the prevention of the thing introduced by it, not the prevention of what it is conjoined to. He mentioned it within its scope only to signal that it is the cause that compelled them to say: ﴿Our Lord, if only You had sent to us a messenger﴾ i.e., why did You not send to us a messenger supported by You with the clear signs?

﴿so that we would follow Your signs﴾ which are manifest through his hand; this is the answer to the second "lawla".

﴿and be among the believers﴾ in them. The answer to the first "lawla" is omitted, relying on the context to indicate it. The meaning: Were it not for their saying this at the time the punishment of their crimes, which they had sent forth, befell them, We would not have sent you. But since their saying that was certain and unavoidable, We sent you, to completely cut off their excuses.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 48:

﴿Then when the truth came to them from Us⁠﴾, that is, the people of Makkah.

﴿The truth from Us⁠﴾, which is the Qur'an revealed to him (ﷺ).

﴿They said⁠﴾, out of obstinacy and making demands: ﴿Why was he not given⁠﴾, meaning him (ﷺ), ﴿the like of what was given to Musa⁠﴾, of the Book revealed all at once. As for the hand and the staff, they have no connection to the matter, like the rest of his (peace be upon him) miracles. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before?⁠﴾ is a refutation of them and a demonstration that what they said was pure obstinacy and not a seeking of that which would guide them to the truth. That is: Did they not, before this statement, disbelieve in what was given to Musa of the Book, just as they disbelieve in this truth? His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿They said⁠﴾ is a resumptive clause brought to establish their disbelief, which is inferred from the preceding denial, and to explain its manner. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Two sorceries⁠﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they mean that what Muhammad was given and what Musa was given, upon them both be peace, are two sorceries.

﴿They support each other⁠﴾, that is, they cooperate by each confirming the other. This is because they sent a group of their men to the rabbis of the Jews at one of their festivals, and they asked them about his (ﷺ) affair. They said: "We find him in the Torah with his description and attributes." When the group returned and informed them of what the Jews had said, they said that. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And they said: Indeed we are, in each⁠﴾, that is, in each one of the two Books, ﴿disbelievers⁠﴾. This is an explicit declaration of their disbelief in both of them, and an emphasis on their disbelief implied by calling them sorcery, and that is due to the utmost of their rebelliousness and their persistence in disbelief and transgression. It has also been read: "two sorcerers who support each other," meaning Musa and Muhammad (ﷺ). This is what the eloquence of the sublime composition demands, so reflect, and set aside what has been said. And it has been said: Do you not see the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 49:

﴿Say: "Then bring a Book from Allah which is better guided than these two, that I may follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ (Mimmā ūtiyāhu) from the Torah and the Qur'an, and you named them two sorceries. For it is explicit regarding what has been mentioned. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that I may follow it﴾ is the answer to the imperative, meaning: if you bring it, I will follow it. Such a condition is of the kind that is uttered by one who relies on the clarity of his proof and the brightness of his path, because bringing something better guided than the two Books is a matter of evident impossibility, so it widens the scope of speech for rebuke and silencing.

﴿If you are truthful﴾, meaning: in your claim that they are two fabricated sorceries. The use of the word "in" (in) together with the impossibility of their being truthful carries a kind of mockery of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 50:

﴿But if they do not respond to you﴾: that is, if they do not do what you have charged them with, namely bringing a Book more guiding than these two, as in His saying, ﴿But if you do not do it﴾. The expression "respond" (istijabah) was used for this to signal that the Prophet (ﷺ) is in complete security about the matter, as if his command to them to bring what was mentioned were a call to them toward an affair whose occurrence he desires. The verb istijabah takes the summoned (al-du'a') directly as its object, and takes the one who calls with the preposition lam. So the summons is usually omitted in that case, and one hardly says, "God responded to his supplication (istajaba Allahu lahu du'a'ahu)."

﴿Then know that they only follow their desires﴾, the false ones, without their having any sound basis at all, since had they had such a basis, they would have produced it.

﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire﴾: this is a rhetorical interrogative of denial (istifham inkari li-l-nafy), meaning: none is more astray than one who follows his desire.

﴿without guidance from God﴾: that is, he is more astray than every astray person. Although the surface composition negates the very essence (of being more astray), not merely the degree of its vices, as has been noted repeatedly in its parallels. Qualifying the following of desire with the absence of guidance from God, exalted is He, serves to intensify the rebuke, to heighten the denunciation and the charge of misguidance. Otherwise, the combination of following desire with His guidance is clearly impossible.

﴿Indeed God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: those who wronged themselves by immersing themselves in following desire and turning away from the signs that guide to the clear truth.

And We have indeed caused the Word to reach them in succession (﴿وَلَقَدْ وصَّلْنا لَهُمُ القَوْلَ﴾). It is also read with the lighter form (wassalnā, bi-l-takhfīf), meaning: We sent down the Qur'an to them continuing, some of it following upon some other, as wisdom and benefit require. Or (it means) consecutively, as promise and warning, narratives, lessons, admonitions and counsels.

﴿لَعَلَّهم يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ — so that they may take heed, and thereby believe in what it contains.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 52:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it﴾ i.e., before the giving of the Qur'an.

﴿They believe in it﴾ They are the believers among the People of the Book. It is said: they were forty from the People of the Gospel, thirty-two of whom came with Ja'far from Abyssinia, and eight from Syria.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 53:

﴿وَإذا يُتْلى﴾ That is: the Qur'an is recited to them.

﴿قالُوا آمَنّا بِهِ إنَّهُ الحَقُّ مِن رَبِّنا﴾ They say: "We have believed in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord." That is: the truth whose veracity we recognise, and this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining what compelled their belief.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنّا كُنّا مِن قَبْلِهِ﴾ "Indeed we were, before it," that is: before its revelation.

﴿مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ "...submitting [to God]" is an explanation that their belief in it was a matter of long standing, since they had witnessed mention of it in the earlier Scriptures, and that they were upon the religion of Islam before the Qur'an was revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 54:

﴿Those﴾ are the ones described by the attributes mentioned. (p-19) ﴿They will be given their reward twice﴾: once for their faith in their own Scripture, and once for their faith in the Qur'an.

﴿Because they endured﴾: for their patience and steadfastness upon both faiths; or upon their faith in the Qur'an before its revelation and after it; or upon the harm inflicted on them by their own religious community who migrated away from them, and by the polytheists.

﴿And they repel evil with good﴾: that is, they repel disobedience with obedience, in accordance with his saying ﷺ: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed, and it will erase it."

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ in the way of goodness.

﴿And when they hear idle talk﴾ from the *ghayn* (the Arabic text reads *min al-ghayn*), ﴿they turn away from it﴾, away from idle talk, out of nobility of character. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾.

﴿And they say﴾ to them, ﴿"For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you"﴾, in a manner of parting ways (*al-mutarakah*) and farewell (*al-tawdi'*, taking leave).

﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾: we do not seek their company, nor do we desire to mix with them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 56:

﴿Indeed, you do not guide﴾ with a guidance that inevitably leads to the desired end, ﴿whom you love﴾ from among people. You are not able to bring him into Islam, even if you exert the utmost effort in this and go beyond every known limit in striving.

﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ to be guided, so that He brings him into Islam.

﴿And He knows best those who are guided﴾, that is, those who are prepared for that. The majority of scholars hold that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. When he was on his deathbed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to him and said to him: "O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, a word by which I may argue on your behalf before Allah." He said to him: "O son of my brother, I know that you are truthful, but I dislike that it be said that he panicked at death. Had it not been that there would be reproach upon you and upon the sons of your father after me, I would have said it, and I would have gladdened your eye with it at parting, because of what I see of your intense grief and your sincere counsel. But I will die upon the religion of the elders, ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Hashim, and ʿAbd Manaf."

﴿And they say: "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land."﴾ It was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn 'Uthman ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf, when he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "We know that you are upon the truth, but we fear that if we follow you and oppose the Arabs, and we are merely a handful (ʾakalat raʾs), they will snatch us away from our land." So He answered them with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾ That is: Did We not protect them, and did We not make their place a sanctuary of security, because of the sanctity of the Sacred House, around which the Arabs fight one another while they themselves are secure?

﴿To it are brought﴾. It is also read as (tujbā), meaning: it is gathered and carried to it.

﴿the fruits of every thing﴾, from every direction. This clause is another description of "a sanctuary," removing what might be imagined as harm to them from the cutting off of supplies.

﴿as a provision from Us﴾. If their condition is as they have mentioned, being worshippers of idols, then how do they fear being snatched away when they combine with the sanctity of the House the sanctity of monotheism?! ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, that is, they are ignorant and do not perceive this, nor do they reflect so that they might know it. It has also been said that it is connected to His saying, "from Us": that is, a few of them reflect and thereby know that this is a provision from Allah, may He be exalted, for had they known, they would not have feared anyone other than Him. The accusative of "rizqan" is either a verbal noun emphasizing the meaning of "yujbā," or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from "thamarāt," on the basis that it carries the meaning of "marzūq" (provided), since it is specified by the annexation. Then He made clear that the matter is the reverse (p-20) and that they are more deserving of fearing the might (baʾs) of Allah, may He be exalted, by His saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 58:

﴿And how many a town have We destroyed, which exulted in its livelihood.﴾ That is: many a people of a town whose condition was like the condition of these (people) in security, comfortable living and ease, until they became insolent, so We brought destruction upon them and laid waste their dwellings.
