﴿So those are their dwellings﴾ left in ruins because of what they did wrong.

﴿Not inhabited after them﴾ after their destruction.

﴿except for a little﴾ That is: except for a little time, since no one lives in them except passing travelers for a day, or part of a day, or there remained none to inhabit them except a few, because of the ill omen of their sins.

﴿And We were the inheritors﴾ of them, since no one succeeded them to manage their dwellings and the rest of their property in the way they did. The accusative of maʿīshatahā (ma'ishatuha, "their livelihood") is either by removal of the preposition (i.e., "in/regarding their livelihood"), or one makes it an adverb of time in itself, as in your saying: Zaid ẓannī muqīm (Zayd is, in my estimation, residing). Or it is by supposing an omitted time noun governing it as its complement, or one makes it an object of baṭirat (bataratha, "exulted") by including the meaning of kafarat (kafarat, "ungratefully rejected").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 59:

﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns﴾ is an explanation of the Divine care (al-'inayah al-rabbaniyyah) following the explanation of the destruction of the aforementioned towns. That is: it was not valid, nor proper; rather, it is impossible within His custom (sunnah), which is founded upon consummate wisdoms. Or: it was not in His past judgment and prior decree that He would destroy the towns before a warning (al-indhar), but rather His habit was that He would not destroy them.

﴿until He raises in their mother (ummiha)﴾ That is: in its origin and its metropolis (qasabatiha), which are its affairs and what follows from them, because its people are more discerning and more noble.

﴿a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾ which speak the truth, and calling them to it by means of encouragement (al-targhib) and warning (al-tarhib). This is in order to establish the proof (ilzam al-hujjah) and cut off excuse, so that they would not say: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger that we might follow Your verses?﴾ The shift to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) is to cultivate awe and to bring in dread. His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We would never destroy the towns﴾ is coordinated with "your Lord would never," and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except when its people are wrongdoers﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances. That is: We would not destroy the people of the towns after We had raised in their mother a messenger calling them to the truth and guiding them to it, in any circumstance, except in the circumstance of their being wrongdoers by denying Our messenger and disbelieving in Our verses. Thus the raising (al-ba'th) is a limit (ghayah) for the impossibility of destruction according to the divine custom, not for its non-occurrence, such that it would entail the realization of destruction immediately following the raising. Its verification has already passed in the commentary on Surat Bani Isra'il.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 60:

﴿And whatever you have been given of a thing﴾, of the matters of this world.

﴿Then it is the enjoyment of the life of this world and its adornment﴾, i.e., it is a thing whose nature is to be enjoyed and adorned with for a few days.

﴿But what is with Allah﴾, which is the reward,

﴿is better﴾ in itself than that, because it is a pure pleasure free from any admixture of pain, and a complete delight free from the mark of anxiety.

﴿And more lasting﴾, because it is everlasting.

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ Will you not reflect so that you would understand this clear matter, and thus exchange what is lower for what is better? It was also read with the yaʼ (ya-taʻqilūn, "will they not reason"), as an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) founded on the fact that the evil of their conduct calls for turning away from addressing them directly.

(p-21) ﴿Is one to whom We have made a fair promise, and who will surely meet it,﴾ i.e., a promise of Paradise, for the goodness of a promise lies in the goodness of what is promised.

﴿then he is one who will surely meet it﴾, i.e., one who will certainly attain it, because of the impossibility of breaking God's promise, the Exalted. For this reason the nominal sentence was used, which conveys that its realization is absolutely certain, and it was joined with the particle "fa" (then), which indicates the meaning of causation.

﴿like one whom We have given the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾, which is mixed with pains, troubled by distress, and which entails regret at its ending. The meaning of the first "fa" (then) is the sequencing of the denial of any resemblance between the people of this world and the people of the Hereafter upon what precedes it, namely the manifest disparity between the enjoyment of the life of this world and what is with God, the Exalted. That is: after this manifest disparity, are the two groups to be placed on equal footing?

God's words ﴿then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forward﴾ are a conjunction with "We have given him enjoyment" and are included together with it within the scope of the relative clause. They emphasize the denial of resemblance and confirm it, as if it were said: "like one whom We have given the enjoyment of the life of this world, then We will bring him forth, or We have brought him forth on the Day of Resurrection, to the Fire, or to the punishment." The choice of the nominal sentence serves to indicate certainty and definitive realization, and placing him among those brought forward carries a dread that is not hidden. The "thumma" (then) indicates temporal or rank-based sequence. It has been read: (thumma hwa) with the ha pronounced with a sukun, likening the separated pronoun to the connected one.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 62:

﴿And [mention] the day He will call to them﴾ is in the accusative by way of coordination (ʿaṭf) with "the Day of Resurrection" (yawm al-qiyāmah), because the two differ in their designation (ʿunwān) even though they are identical in their referent (dhāt), or it is governed by an implied "remember" (idhkur).

﴿Then He will say﴾ is an explanation of the calling (nidāʾ). ﴿"Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ That is: those whom you used to claim to be My partners. Both objects have been omitted together, relying on the context to indicate them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 63:

﴿Those against whom the Word has been justified will say﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), built upon the narration of the question, as if it were said: "What then issued from them at that time?" So it was said: "Those against whom the Word has been justified will say," and they are their associates from among the devils, or their leaders who were taken as lords besides Allah, Exalted is He, by obeying them in everything they commanded them and forbade them. The meaning of "the Word has been justified against them" is that its requirement has become established and its consequence has been realized. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾, and other verses of warning. Their being singled out for this ruling, although it also includes the followers, is because of their originality in disbelief and their deserving of punishment, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them"﴾. Their hastening to answer, although the question was addressed to the worshippers, is either because they perceived that the question about them was to bring them to mind and to rebuke them for misguidance, and they were certain that the worshippers would say, "These are the ones who misled us," or because the worshippers had said it as an excuse, or these only said what they said in reply to their statement. However, the saying of the worshippers was not related, for brevity, since it was evident.

﴿"Our Lord, these are the ones whom we misled"﴾ That is: they are the ones whom we misled, so the returning pronoun to the relative was omitted. Their purpose in using the demonstrative is to make clear that they are saying what they say in the presence of those (the followers), and that they are unable to deny it or refute it. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"We misled them as we ourselves were misled"﴾ is the answer in reality, and what precedes it is a preparation for it, meaning: (p-22) we did not compel them into error; we only misled them by way of whispering and enticement, not by force and compulsion. So they went astray by their own choice, a going astray like our going astray by our own choice. It is also permissible that "the ones" (alladhina) be an attribute of the demonstrative, and "we misled them" be the predicate.

﴿"We disown before You"﴾ of them, and of what they chose of disbelief and sins by their own desire. This is an affirmation of what precedes it, and for that reason it is not joined to it by a conjunction. Likewise His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"They were not worshipping us"﴾, that is: they were not worshipping us, but were worshipping their own desires. It has also been said that "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle connected to His saying, Exalted is He, "We disown," meaning: we disown their worship of us.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 64:

﴿And it will be said: "Call upon your partners."﴾ Either in mockery of them, or as a rebuke to them.

﴿Then they will call upon them﴾ out of extreme bewilderment.

﴿But they will not respond to them﴾ because it is necessary that they lack the ability to respond and to give help.

﴿And they will see the punishment﴾ having already overwhelmed them, ﴿if only they had been guided﴾ to some means of the stratagems by which they could ward off the punishment, or to the truth, when they encounter what they encounter. It has also been said: "law" (law, "if only") here expresses a wish, meaning: they will wish that they had been guided.

﴿And on the Day He calls them and says, "What was your response to the messengers?"﴾ This is coordinated with what precedes it: they were first asked about their associating (partners with God), and second about their response to the messengers who had forbidden them from that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 66:

﴿Then the news became obscure to them on that day, like blindness to them, [so] they could not find their way to them.﴾ That is: it became like blindness to them, so that they could not be guided to them. The original form was "they were blinded to the news" (fa-'amu 'an al-anba'), but it was reversed for emphasis and to draw attention to the fact that what is present in the mind overflows onto it and reaches it from outside; so when it errs, there is no way for it to recall it. The verb is followed by "ʿalā" (upon) because it implies the meaning of concealment and confusion. The word "al-anba'" (the news) may refer either to what was asked of them, namely what they answered the Messengers with, or to all news, which is included in it in the first instance. And if the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, delegate knowledge in that terrifying situation to the Knower of the unseen, despite their being free of the extreme of being questioned, then what do you think of those misguided peoples?! ﴿So they will not question one another.﴾ That is, they will not ask one another about the answer, due to the extreme of their bewilderment, or due to knowing that all are alike in ignorance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 67:

﴿Then as for him who repents⁠﴾ from shirk (associating partners with God).

﴿and believes and does righteous deeds⁠﴾, i.e., he combines faith (iman) and righteous action (al-'amal al-salih).

﴿then it is likely that he will be among the successful⁠﴾, i.e., those who attain what is sought with Him, may He be exalted, and who are saved from what is feared. "'Asa" (perhaps, it is likely) here is for certainty, according to the custom of the noble ones; or it expresses hope on the part of the penitent, meaning: let him expect success.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 68:**

﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills﴾, that He create it.

﴿And chooses﴾ whatever He wills to choose, without any obligation upon Him, and without any prohibition on Him at all.

﴿They did not have the choice﴾, i.e., the choosing, like the *tiyara* (omen) in the sense of *tatayyur* (augury). The intended meaning is the negation of influential choice on their part, and this is beyond doubt. It has also been said that the intended meaning is that no one among His creatures may choose over Him. For this reason it is without the conjunction (*al-'atif*, the coordinating particle). This is supported by what is related: it was revealed concerning the statement of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾ The meaning is: Allah the Exalted does not send the messengers by the choice of those to whom they are sent. It has also been said that its meaning is: and He chooses that in which there is good and righteousness for them.

﴿Glory be to Allah﴾, i.e., He is exalted in His essence with a particular exaltation unique to Him, above anyone disputing with Him, or any choice competing with His choice.

﴿And exalted is He above what they associate﴾, above their association (of partners with Him), or above the partnership of what they associate with Him.

Your Lord knows what their breasts conceal, such as their enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and their rancor against him.

And what they disclose, such as their slandering of him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 70:

﴿And He is Allah﴾, that is: the One deserving of worship.

﴿There is no deity except Him﴾: no one deserves it except Him.

﴿To Him belongs praise in the first and the last﴾, because He is the bestower of all blessings, both those that are hastened and those that are deferred, upon all creation without exception. The believers will praise Him in the Hereafter just as they praised Him in this world, by saying: "All praise is due to Allah, who has removed grief from us. All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us," in delight at His bounty and in pleasure at praising Him.

﴿And to Him belongs the judgment﴾, that is: the executed decree over everything, without any partner in it for anyone else.

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ by resurrection, and to no other.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 71:

﴿Say﴾ (a restatement of what was mentioned before).

﴿Tell me﴾: i.e., inform me.

﴿If Allah makes the night perpetual for you﴾ — "sarmadan" (perpetual), from al-sard (al-sardu), which means continuity and persistence. The "mim" in it is an added letter, as in "dulamis," from al-dilas (smoothness): a coat of mail is called "dir'un dilasun," i.e., smooth and soft. ﴿Until the Day of Resurrection﴾ — by keeping the sun beneath the earth, or by moving it around the receding horizon.

﴿What god other than Allah﴾: "min ilahun" is a description of "ilah" (god). ﴿Could bring you light﴾ is another description of it, upon which the matter of rebuke and censure turns, as in the Exalted saying: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?﴾ and the Exalted saying: ﴿Then who would bring you flowing water?﴾ and their like, except that it intends to show the negation of the qualified (the god) by the negation of the quality, and it did not say: "Is there a god...?" etc., in order to present the rebuke and censure according to their claim. It was also read as "bi-diya'in" with two hamzas.

﴿Will you not then hear﴾ this true statement with the hearing of reflection and insight, so that you submit to it and act in accordance with its requirement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 72:

﴿Say: Have you considered: if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection﴾ by holding it still in the midst of the sky, or by moving it on an orbit above the horizon.

﴿Who is a god other than Allah who could bring you a night in which you may rest?﴾ (seeking respite from the fatigue of occupations). The omission of mention of the benefits of light may be because it is intended for its own sake, and its following upon the benefits attached to it is evident.

﴿Will you not then see?﴾ This is the evident benefit, which is not hidden from anyone who has sight.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 73:

﴿And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein﴾: that is, in the night.

﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾: in the day, through various kinds of gain.

﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾: so that you may be grateful for His blessing, may He be exalted, for doing what He did; or so that you may recognize His blessing, may He be exalted, and thank Him for it.

And the day He calls to them, He will say: "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?" (Quoted from the verse: ﴿And the day He calls to them﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "remember" (udhkur) understood.) ﴿Where are My partners whom you used to claim﴾ is a rebuke following upon a rebuke, to indicate that nothing brings about the anger of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, more than associating partners with Him (shirk), just as nothing brings about His pleasure more than affirming His oneness (tawhid), glorified is He. And the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 75:

﴿And We shall draw out﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to "yunadihim" (He calls them). The use of the past form (ṣīghat al-māḍī) serves to indicate certainty (al-taḥaqquq), or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its subject, with "qad" implied. The shift to the first-person plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah) serves to show the utmost concern with the matter of the drawing out and its awesomeness, meaning: We brought out.

﴿from every nation﴾ of the nations ﴿a witness﴾, a prophet who bears witness against them concerning what they used to be upon, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you against these as a witness?﴾ [4:41]. ﴿Then We shall say﴾ to every nation from those nations.

﴿Bring your proof﴾ for the soundness of what you used to adhere to.

﴿Then they will know﴾ on that day ﴿that the truth belongs to Allah﴾ in divinity, none sharing in it with Him.

﴿And what they used to fabricate will be lost to them﴾, meaning it will be absent from them with the absence of one who is lost, ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾ in the world of falsehood.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 76:

﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa.﴾ He was the paternal cousin of Musa: Yasahar ibn Qahath ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and Musa, peace be upon him, was the son of 'Imran ibn Qahath. It is also said that Musa, peace be upon him, was his cousin's son, and he was called al-Munawwar (the Illuminated) because of the beauty of his appearance. It is also said that he was the most skilled of the Children of Israel in the Torah, but he became a hypocrite just as al-Samiri did, and he said: "If prophethood belongs to Musa, and the altar and the sacrifice belong to Harun, then what is mine?" It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, led them across the sea, and prophethood, the office of the high priesthood (al-Hubbura), and the sacrifice went to Harun, Qarun felt envy in himself and envied both of them. He said to Musa: "The command is yours, and I am of no account. How long must I endure?" Musa, peace be upon him, said: "This is the doing of God, exalted is He." He said: "I will not believe you until you bring a sign." So he ordered the leaders of the Children of Israel that each one should bring a staff, and he bound them together and placed them in the tent in which revelation used to descend to him. They kept guard over their staffs during the night, and in the morning, behold, the staff of Harun was moving and had green leaves. Qarun said: "This is no more wondrous than what you do of sorcery." This is the meaning of His, exalted is He, words: ﴿So he rebelled against them﴾, that is, he sought superiority over them and that they should be under his command, or he wronged them. It is said: that was when Pharaoh made him ruler over the Children of Israel. It is also said: he envied them. This is what was mentioned of him concerning Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both.

﴿And We gave him of the treasures﴾, that is, the stored wealth.

﴿Indeed, its keys﴾, that is, the keys of its chests. It is the plural of miftah (with a kasra), which is that by which something is opened. It is also said: its treasuries; the regular singular of it is al-maftah (with a fatha).

﴿Were a burden to a band of strong men﴾ is the predicate of inna. The clause is the relative clause of "ma," and it is the second object of "atā" (to give). Naʾa bihi al-himl means the load weighed him down until it bent him over. Al-ʿusba and al-ʿusaba mean a large group. It was also read as (layanū'u) with the ya', by giving the mudaf the ruling of the mudaf ilayhi, as passed in His, exalted is He, words: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of God (p-25) is near to the doers of good﴾.

﴿When his people said to him﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "tanū'u." It is also said: governed by "baghā" (rebelled). This was rejected on the ground that rebellion is not restricted to that time. It is also said: governed by "ātaynāhu" (We gave him). This was rejected on the ground that giving is also not restricted to that time. It is also said: governed by a implied verb. Some say it is "udhkur" (remember), and some say it is "adhhara al-farah" (he showed exultation). It is permissible for it to be governed by what follows it from His, exalted is He, words: ﴿He said: "I was given it only﴾, and the clause would then confirm his rebellion.

﴿Do not exult﴾, that is, do not be insolent. Exultation in this world is blameworthy absolutely, because it is the result of loving it, being content with it, and being heedless of its passing away, for knowing that the pleasure in it is inevitably separated from one, necessarily produces sorrow. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not exult in what He has given you﴾. Here He gave as the reason for the prohibition that it prevents one from loving Him, mighty and exalted: ﴿Indeed, God does not love the exultant﴾, that is, those exultant over the adornments of this world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 77:

﴿Wa-btaghi﴾ (and seek). It is also read as (wa-ittabi'), (and follow).

﴿fīmā ātākal-lāh﴾ (in what Allah has given you) of wealth; ﴿al-dār al-ākhirah﴾ (the Hereafter), that is, the reward of Allah Most High therein, which you should direct toward whatever becomes a means to it.

﴿Wa-lā tansa﴾ (and do not forget), that is, do not abandon it in the manner of one who has been forgotten.

﴿naṣībaka min al-dunyā﴾ (your share of this world), which is that you attain your Hereafter through it and take from it what suffices you.

﴿Wa-aḥsin﴾ (and do good), that is, to the servants of Allah Most High.

﴿kamā aḥsanal-lāhu ilayk﴾ (as Allah has been good to you) in what He has bestowed upon you. It is also said: do good by way of thankfulness and obedience, as Allah has been good to you by bestowing favours.

﴿Wa-lā tabghi al-fasāda fil-arḍ﴾ (and do not seek corruption in the earth): a prohibition against the injustice and oppression in which he was engaged.

﴿Inna-llāha lā yuḥibbu al-mufsidīn﴾ (indeed Allah does not love the corrupters) because of the evil of their deeds.

﴿He said﴾, replying to his advisers, ﴿"I have only been given it on knowledge I possess."﴾ It seems he intends by this a rebuttal of their saying, ﴿"As Allah has been good to you."﴾ This is because it informs that He, exalted, bestowed upon him those wealths and treasures without any cause or entitlement on his part. That is, "I was preferred by it over people, and deserved by it to excel over them in wealth and standing." "On knowledge" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). This knowledge is the knowledge of the Tawrat (Torah), and he was the most knowledgeable of them in it. It was also said that it was the knowledge of kimiya' (alchemy). It was said that it was the knowledge of carpentry and dahqana (agriculture and landholding), and all other means of earning. It was also said that it was the knowledge of opening treasures and hidden hoards. "ʿindī" ("in my possession") is either an attribute of "ʿilm," or it is related to "ūtītuhu" ("I have been given it"), as in your saying: "this passed (or was valid) according to me," or "in my opinion and view."

﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations that were stronger than him in might and greater in accumulation?﴾ This is a rebuke to him from Allah, exalted, for his being deceived by his strength and abundance of wealth, despite his knowing this through reading the Torah, receiving it from Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, and hearing it from transmitters of histories. It is also an expression of wonder at him. The meaning is: did he not read the Torah, and did he not know what Allah, exalted, did to the likes of him among the peoples of earlier generations, so that he would not be deceived as they were deceived? This was raised because of his claim to knowledge and his magnifying himself by it, so the knowledge is negated from him. The meaning is: does he know what he claimed, yet not know this, so that he might save himself from the fates of the perished?

﴿And the guilty will not be asked about their sins﴾. This is not a question of inquiry; rather, they will be punished for them suddenly. It is as if Qarun, when he was threatened by the mention of the destruction of those before him who were stronger and wealthier than him, was reinforced in this by the explanation that this was not something specific to those who were destroyed. Rather, Allah, exalted, is aware of the sins of all the guilty, and He will certainly punish them for them.

(p-26) ﴿So he went out to his people⦆ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "qāla" (he said), and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ). His words, ﴿in his adornment⦆, may be connected either to "kharaja" (went out) or to a deleted element; it is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) referring to its subject, meaning: he went out upon them existing in his adornment. It is said: he went out mounted on a grey mule, upon which was a saddle-cloth of crimson (al-urjuwān), and its saddle was of gold, and with him were four thousand [attendants] in his attire. It is also said: upon them and upon their horses were red brocade (al-dībāj al-aḥmar), and on his right were three hundred boys, and on his left three hundred white maidens, adorned with jewelry and brocade. It is also said: he went out among ninety thousand, upon them were safflower-dyed garments (al-muʿaṣfarāt), and this was the first day on which saffron-dyed clothing was seen (rū'iya, "was seen" in the sense of became notable).

﴿Those who desired the life of this world⦆ said, among the believers, in accordance with the customs of human nature regarding the desire for abundance and ease.

﴿Would that we had the like of what Qarun was given!⦆ It is reported from Qatadah that they wished for it so that they might draw near to God Most High by it and spend it in the ways of goodness. It is also said that those who made this wish were a people of disbelievers.

﴿Indeed, he is truly possessed of a great fortune⦆ is an explanation (taʿlīl) for their wish and an emphasis (taʾkīd) upon it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 80:

﴿And those who had been given knowledge said﴾ i.e., of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter as they ought to be known. The reason they are not described as desiring the reward of the Hereafter is to draw attention to the fact that knowledge of the conditions of the two abodes necessarily entails turning away from the first and turning decisively toward the second, and that the wishing of those who wish (for the riches of Qarun) is only due to their not knowing the two as they ought to be known.

﴿Woe to you!﴾ (waylakum) is an invocation of destruction, which has come into common use as a rebuke against what is not approved.

﴿The reward of Allah﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is better﴾ than what you wish for ﴿for those who believe and do righteous deeds.﴾ So it is not fitting for you to wish for it while not being content with the reward from the Exalted.

﴿But none receives it﴾ (wa la yulaqqaha) i.e., this statement which the scholars uttered, or the reward, for it carries the meaning of recompense, or Paradise, or faith and righteous deeds, for these two carry the meaning of conduct and way. ﴿except the patient﴾ i.e., patient in obedience and in refraining from desires.

He was narrated to have constantly harmed Musa (peace be upon him), while Musa tolerated him because of their kinship, until the zakat (the obligatory alms, a levy on wealth) was revealed. Musa (peace be upon him) then reached an agreement with him that one out of every thousand would be taken as zakat. Qarun calculated it and considered it too much, so he resolved to disgrace Musa (peace be upon him) among the Children of Israel. He offered one of their prostitutes a thousand dinars, and it was said a gold basin filled with gold. On a day of festival, Musa (peace be upon him) stood to deliver a sermon and said: "Whoever steals, we will cut off his hand; whoever commits fornication while unmarried, we will flog; and whoever commits fornication while married, we will stone."

Qarun said: "Even if you are the one?" He said: "Even if I am the one." Qarun said: "The Children of Israel claim that you committed fornication with so-and-so." She was brought in, and he (peace be upon him) adjured her to tell the truth. She said: "Qarun offered me a reward on condition that I accuse you with myself." Musa (peace be upon him) fell down in prostration before his Lord, weeping, and said: "My Lord, if I am Your messenger, then be angry on my behalf." It was revealed to him: "Command the earth to do whatever you wish, for it is obedient to you."

He said: "O Children of Israel, God has sent me to Qarun just as He sent me to Pharaoh. Whoever is with him, let him remain in his place, and whoever is with me, let him withdraw from him." They all withdrew except two men. Then he said: "O earth, seize them!" It seized them up to the knees. Then he said: "Seize them!" It seized them up to the waists. Then he said: "Seize them!" It seized them up to the necks. They were appealing to him (peace and blessings be upon him) by God Most High and by kinship, but he did not turn to them because of the intensity of his anger. Then he said: "Seize them!" and it closed over them. The Children of Israel woke up whispering among themselves: "Musa (peace be upon him) only prayed against him so that he could seize his house and treasures." So he called upon God Most High until his house and his wealth were swallowed up.

﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling﴾. ﴿Then he had no group﴾, a sympathetic company, ﴿who could help him against God﴾ by averting the punishment from him.

﴿Nor was he among those who could defend themselves﴾: that is, those who protect themselves from it in any way. It is said: "He helped him against his enemy and he defended himself," meaning he prevented him and he refrained.

And those who had wished for his position ﴿وَأصْبَحَ الَّذِينَ تَمَنَّوْا مَكانَهُ﴾ his station ﴿بِالأمْسِ﴾ yesterday, meaning since a recent time.

﴿يَقُولُونَ ويْكَأنَّ اللَّهَ يَبْسُطُ الرِّزْقَ لِمَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ ويَقْدِرُ﴾ They say: "Wayka'anna Allah extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants, and restricts it." That is, He does each of extending and restricting by His sheer will, not because of a honour that requires extension, nor because of a humiliation that requires restriction. According to the Basrans (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), wayka'anna is composed of wai (وَيْ), expressing wonder (lil-ta'ajjub), and ka'anna (كَأنَّ), expressing comparison (lil-tashbih). The meaning is: "How much the matter resembles that Allah extends..." etc. According to the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun, the grammarians of Kufa), it is from wayka (وَيْكَ) meaning "woe to you" (waylaka), and anna (أنَّ). Its implied sense is: "Wayka, know that Allah..." It is used when alerting someone to an error and expressing regret. The meaning is that they had become aware of their error in wishing, and regretted it.

﴿لَوْلا أنْ مَنَّ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنا﴾ Had Allah not bestowed His favour upon us, by not giving us what we had wished for, and giving us the like of what He gave him, ... Among the Qur'anic readings (qira'at, recited variants) it is read: (لَوْلا مَنَّ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنا لَخَسَفَ بِنا كَما خَسَفَ بِهِ), "Had Allah's favour not been upon us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us as He caused it to swallow him." It is also read: (لَخُسِفَ بِنا), in the passive voice, with بِنا serving as the deputy subject (al-qa'im maqam al-fa'il). It is also read: (لانْخَسَفَ بِنا), like your saying: أنْقَطَعَ بِهِ (anqata'a bihi, "he was cut off"), and it is read: (لَتُخُسِّفَ بِنا).

﴿وَيْكَأنَّهُ لا يُفْلِحُ الكافِرُونَ﴾ "And wayka'annahu, the disbelievers will not prosper," meaning those who are ungrateful for the blessing of Allah the Exalted, or those who deny His messengers and what they were promised of the reward of the Hereafter.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 83:**

﴿That is the Last Abode⦆ — this is a demonstrative of glorification and magnification, as if it were said: "That is the one whose report you have heard, and whose description has reached you."

﴿We shall assign it to those who do not desire exaltation (ʿulūw) in the earth﴾ — that is: dominance and domination.

﴿Nor corruption﴾ — that is: oppression and transgression against the servants, like the practice of Pharaoh and Qarun. In making the promise conditional on abandoning their desire for these two, rather than on abandoning the two themselves, there is an added warning against them. It is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man may be pleased that the thong of his sandal is finer than the thong of his companion's sandal, and so he enters under it (into the category of this warning).

﴿And the good end﴾ — the praiseworthy one — ﴿is for the God-fearing﴾, that is: those who guard against what Allah the Exalted does not approve of, in deeds and in words.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 84:

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him﴾ — in return for it — ﴿is better than it﴾ — in essence, in attribute, and in measure.

﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except with what they used to do.﴾ Here the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is placed, and the apparent noun is used in place of the pronoun, in order to denounce their condition by repeating the attribution of evil deeds to them.

﴿Except what they used to do﴾ — that is, except the like of what they used to do. The word "the like" (al-mithl) has been omitted and what they used to do has been put in its place, as an intensification of the equivalence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 85:

(p-28) ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained the Qur'an for you﴾ made it obligatory upon you to recite it, to convey it, and to act upon it.

﴿Will surely bring you back to a return (ma'ad)﴾. That is, to a return (ma'ad): a return toward which the necks of aspirations stretch, and toward which the eyes of nations gaze, and it is the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud) in which He promised to resurrect you. It was also said that it is Makkah the Honored, because He, exalted is He, had promised him, while he was in Makkah suffering harm and hardship from its people, that He would make him emigrate from it and then return him to it with manifest honor and overpowering authority. It was also said: it was revealed to him when he reached al-Juhfah on his migration, having longed for his birthplace, the birthplace of his forefathers, and the sanctuary of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). So Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and said to him: "Do you long for Makkah?" He said: "Yes." So he revealed it to him.

﴿Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance﴾ and who deserves reward and victory. The word "man" (who) is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied by "a'lam" (knows best), meaning: "He knows." It was also said that it is governed by "a'lam" itself, on the basis that it carries the meaning of "knowing" (ʿālim).

﴿And who is in manifest error﴾ and who deserves punishment and humiliation. By this he means himself and the polytheists. This is a confirmation of the preceding threat. Likewise His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 86:

﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be sent down to you﴾ — i.e., He will return you to your place of return (ma'ad), just as the Book was sent down to you, though you had not hoped for it.

﴿Except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ — but He sent it down to you as a mercy from Him. It is also permissible that this be an exception (istithna') construed according to the sense (mahmul 'ala al-ma'na), as if it were said: "The Book was not sent down to you except as a mercy," meaning: for the sake of showing mercy.

﴿So never be a supporter (zahir) to the disbelievers﴾ — by flattering them (mudara), bearing their burdens on their behalf, and responding to their requests.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 87:

﴿And let them not turn you away﴾ from (i.e., the disbelievers).

﴿from the signs of Allah﴾ i.e., from reciting them and acting upon them.

﴿after they have been revealed to you﴾ and enjoined upon you. It is also read as (yuṣiddunnaka), from aṣadda, the transitive form derived from ṣadda (the intransitive).

﴿And call﴾ people ﴿to your Lord﴾, to His worship and His unification (tawhid).

﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ by assisting them in their affairs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 28, verse 88:

﴿And do not call upon another god along with Allah.﴾ This and what precedes it are for stirring up and inciting (al-tahyij wal-ilhab), and for cutting off the hopes of the polytheists of obtaining his (ﷺ) assistance in it, and for showing that the thing forbidden is so ugly and evil that it is forbidden to one from whom its occurrence is not possible at all.

﴿There is no god but Him﴾ alone. ﴿Everything perishes except His Face﴾, except His Essence, for everything other than Him, whatever it may be, is in its own essence contingent (mumkin) and exposed to perishing and non-existence.

﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾, that is, the binding decree over creation.

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ at the Resurrection, for recompense with truth and justice. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Ta-Sin-Mim al-Qasas, he will have a reward equal to the number of those who believed in Musa and those who denied him, and no angel in the heavens and the earth will remain but that it will testify for him on the Day of Resurrection that he was truthful."
